did_you_know.text: The LORD recalls the Exodus from Egypt and describes Egypt as a “furnace of iron”—an image of a place of harsh oppression. As part of the covenant, the people were required to obey the LORD and follow His commandments.
The purpose of the covenant was to fulfill the oath the LORD swore to the ancestors and to give them a land “flowing with milk and honey.” Jeremiah responds to these words by saying, “Amen, LORD.”
The LORD describes His warnings to the people as an ongoing action: from the day He brought their ancestors out of Egypt until Jeremiah’s time, He repeatedly warned them and called them to obey Him.
The people are described as having returned to the sins of their ancestors: Israel and Judah worshiped other gods and broke the covenant the LORD had made with their ancestors.
The extent of their idolatry is illustrated by the number of altars: Judah had as many gods as it had cities, and Jerusalem had as many altars as it had streets, where incense was burned to Baal.

Jeremiah is commanded not to pray for the people or offer cries and prayers on their behalf, because the LORD says He will not listen to them when disaster comes upon them, after the evil they have done.

The LORD reveals the plot against Jeremiah, and only after this revelation does he understand what the people of Anathoth have done. In this way, the chapter portrays the prophet as unaware of the conspiracy being formed against him.
Jeremiah compares himself to “a gentle lamb led to the slaughter,” because the people of Anathoth planned to harm him without his knowing it.
The people of Anathoth told Jeremiah not to prophesy in the name of the LORD and threatened to kill him if he continued. The chapter presents opposition to the prophet coming from his own town.

The punishment announced for the people of Anathoth includes the sword for the young men and famine for the sons and daughters. In the end, it is said that they will have no survivors in the year of their punishment.
